- **Verify r6 (census adequacy, the closure: every r5 fix reverted on a copy, one part at a time, and the gate that turns red named).** The fast census's repaint rows now check everything their labels name: the Task Group detail window's repaint while a field is being typed in, Session Properties' repaint while a select has the focus, and the live For-you arrival toast's re-wording — one of them was written so that it passed on half of its claim, the others checked only that the window listened. Each is reverted on a copy in the census itself and turns exactly its own row red. Two more places could bring cleared words back when the browser reconnected at the moment of a clear (reproduced by dropping the connection for real and holding the page's older answers until after the clear): a session's card in the sidebar showed a cleared current status again (and kept it until some other status changed), and the Channels panel showed a cleared group message again as the group's last line. Both now ignore an answer that is older than an update they already received. An agent group's window opened (or restored on another device) at the moment a message was cleared showed the message's words: it ignored the clear until its first page had arrived, and that page had been read before the clear. It now keeps the clear from the moment it opens. The class these three belong to — an answer read before a clear, shown after it — now has its own gates: the fast census lists every place the page fetches one of the five stores and requires the check that drops an older answer (a new place is refused until it says which), and the browser census clears with such answers deliberately in flight (the connection dropped for real, the windows mid-refresh) — the one r5 fix that no test noticed when it was taken out (Session Properties' history painting whichever answer came last) is now caught by both. The status box you open from a session's state chip or Session Properties ("Change…") no longer brings back a reason that was cleared while it was open: pressing Apply to change only the state used to save the old words again as your own status; an untouched Reason box now follows the current record. Folding a group of Background Work jobs saved the jobs' NAME in your account's saved preferences on the server (every device, a configuration export), and clearing the job did not reach it: the fold is now remembered by a fingerprint of the name, and an older saved entry is dropped (that group's fold goes back to its default once).
- **Verify r7 (the final closure, fresh eyes; each finding reproduced in Chrome first, fixed and pinned with a pre-fix copy as the control).** A layout you saved by name while a background job's "Job input" window was open — or the layout of a desktop you had switched away from — kept that job's name in the page's memory after the job was cleared (never shown, never sent; gone at the next reload): the page now records such a window under its generic title the moment it captures a layout, from the same table the server uses. Every other place your browser's state is saved on the server — drafts, settings, uploads, the stage, bookmarks, themes, every section of a config backup, diagnostics, incident captures, the ops log, each session's sidecar files — was exported and searched after a clear and holds none of the words; each is now listed in the census with what proves it, and the release gate's walk exports a backup with every section after the clear. The For-you popup, once closed (a click anywhere else closes it — including the right-click that opens "Clear content…" on another window), kept its rows in the page: a record cleared while it was closed stayed there unseen until the popup was opened again; the popup now empties itself when it closes (a reply you were typing is kept as a draft). Double-clicking a background job's Start answered "<job name> is already running", and that message stayed in the For-you Notifications tab after the job was cleared: Background Work now names the job by its id in such a message.
- **Verify r8 (the interpolation census: every message that repeats a record's words, found from the code — not one more example).** A new part of the fast census reads every toast, dialog, window title, server notice, telemetry event, error and refusal sentence, For-you item made from another record, delivery into a conversation and browser console line in the whole code base, and fails any that repeats a cleared kind's words in a place a clear cannot reach (a toast's history, the Diagnostics window, a log). It found one: trying to mount a port at a /svc/ path another forward already used named that forward by its label — for a background job's service, the job's name — and the refusal stayed in the Notifications tab after the job was cleared; it now names the machine and port instead. Clearing a published service's job right after a restart (before the service was published again) left the job's name on its port forward in the Ports panel — the forward is now found by its label. An incident captured after a job was cleared (including the automatic capture when the page freezes) could still carry the job's name, because the server's recent log lines ride along in every incident and some of them named jobs — log lines now name a job by its id. A port scan in the Ports panel (which tags a listening port with its background job's name) kept that name after the job was cleared, until the next scan or a reload — the scan now forgets it at the clear. The Ports panel showed a cleared service's label in English on a Chinese or Japanese page; it now uses the page's language.
- **Verify r9 (the short closure: r8's fixes reverted one part at a time, the census's declared gaps measured).** A Background Work job that takes back its conversation's draft while that conversation is not running is recorded as the conversation, not by the job's name — the name stayed on the draft's record after the job was cleared. Clearing a published service no longer relabels the port forward of a different service that happens to have the same name. …nor replaces with the cleared sentence a same-named job's notification that is still waiting to reach its conversation. The server no longer keeps the text of the last agent message or Background Work notification it sent in memory (it keeps a fingerprint to spot a repeat), so a cleared message or job leaves no copy there.
- **The reader census (test-record-clear-census, fast) and the runtime walk (test-record-clear-walk, heavy).** Every code path that can carry one of the five stores' words to a client, an agent, a file or another machine is derived from the tree by grep and judged against one table: each store's data file is named by its owner module only; every read of the append-only group log is folded, the clear's own, or gated off the groups adapter; every store-touching route (60) is classified — 18 read record text and 2 read the folded group log, and each of those is exercised by the walk; the five broadcasts, the five CLIs, the derived copies each door rewrites, and twelve declared exceptions with their reasons (the group log's own file and a run's own log file are append-only; delivered words in transcripts; the user's own exports). Four patched copies, each adding one raw reader, turn the census red on exactly their leg. The walk boots a server with every record carrying its own word, proves every reader shows it, tries the owner's door under every token kind and the agent's reach at every boundary, clears everything, and finds no word anywhere afterwards — routes, injections, CLIs, broadcasts, the session's own stdin, the journal, and on disk only the two declared holders.
- Gates: test-record-clear (fast, in-process: the rule and the cleared record as tables, eight patched-copy controls), test-record-clear-stores (fast, in-process: the five real stores, the owner routes, the agent verbs and the real `vibespace-task` / `vibespace-ask` against a stub server — every copy of a planted marker gone, every journal line ids-only; verify r3's six legs with their controls), test-record-clear-census (fast: the reader census with four controls), test-record-clear-ui (heavy, chrome: the five menus with real right-clicks and every visible door pressed for real, the batch — and a 250-entry one —, a second client in Chinese patched live, a third in Japanese, the dialog inside the viewport on a desktop and a phone), test-record-clear-walk (heavy: the runtime sentinel walk over a real server).

### Channels: rich messages read as they were written (lane channel-rich, the owner's report 2026-09-28)

- **A Gmail message that has an HTML part is shown FORMATTED by default** (邮件按原来的格式显示) — headings, bold, lists, tables, links, the pictures that are part of the mail itself. The owner: "gmail 这种富文本 html 内容似乎完全没有按照 html 渲染". Every such message has a small **Formatted | Plain text** switch (格式化 | 纯文本); your choice for a message stays while the window is open. A message with no HTML part looks exactly as before.
- **Remote pictures are blocked until you press "Show pictures" on that message** (显示图片) — a mail client's rule: a tracking picture tells the sender you read the mail. Pressing it shows that sender's pictures for the rest of this browser session, never for everyone and never stored.
- **The formatted mail can never touch VibeSpace.** It is drawn inside a fully sealed frame (`sandbox="allow-scripts"` only — no same origin, no forms, no pop-ups, no navigation); the mail's HTML is cleaned twice (our own allowlist writer, then DOMPurify) and the frame carries a strict Content-Security-Policy, so scripts, forms, embedded frames, `javascript:` links and CSS that tries to load something are all gone. A link you click opens in a new tab only if it is a web or mail address. The only thing the page takes from the frame is its height.
- **A long thread stays light**: a formatted mail is drawn only while it is on screen (at most 6 at once); scrolling away frees it.
- **A thread reads as its new words** (naive-user verify): the quoted history a reply carries (Gmail's, Apple Mail's, Thunderbird's, Yahoo's own quote blocks) is folded behind "Show quoted text" inside the formatted mail, as the plain-text view already folds it — a 10-mail thread no longer opens on a wall of quoted mail. **A wide newsletter fits the phone**: a mail wider than its frame is scaled down to fit instead of being cut off on the right. The Formatted | Plain text switch stays above the message in both views (it used to jump under the text when you pressed Plain text).
- **A hostile mail or Lark message can no longer freeze VibeSpace** (security verify): a mail built to make the cleaner work quadratically (an HTML tag that never closes, a style full of `url(` with no `)`) is cleaned in a fraction of a second at its 2 MB limit instead of freezing the tab for minutes; a Lark message with a tag full of spaces or thousands of unclosed code fences no longer stalls the server for seconds at every read; a Lark message nested thousands of quotes deep no longer breaks the reading of its whole conversation; a formatted body the server says is over the size limit is never downloaded.
- **Agents never receive HTML** — an agent's `read` / `search`, the preview line, the attention list and search keep using the message's text.
- **A Gmail mail with only an HTML part no longer stalls the server while it is read** (security verify round 2): the words an agent reads from an HTML-only mail (and the sender's address) were produced by regexes that re-scanned the whole part for every `<` — 64 KB of `<` cost 1.2 s, 128 KB 4.7 s of the server's event loop at ingest, with no size bound at all (a From header of 64 KB of `<`: 1.4 s). Both are now one bounded walk. Gate: the new **test-peer-parsers** census — every parser of peer bytes in the channel modules has a size cap and is linear on its own adversarial shapes, a new one goes red until placed; three restored quadratic loops go red as controls.
- **A long Lark rich-text post no longer stalls the server** (security verify round 2): a post element with thousands of list items or line breaks made the reader re-read the text it had just built on every item (128 KB of `<li>` = 0.43 s of the event loop at ingest, a megabyte half a minute), and a post element's text had no size bound at all. The reader now keeps one character beside the text instead of re-reading it, and a post element's text is bounded like every other body. Gate: test-channel-blocks ⑱.
- **A Lark message that mentions a tag word no longer loses its tail** (security verify round 2): "please set the <title> of the page to Foo" was read as "please set the" — the reader took `<title>` (and `<script>`, `<style>`, `<select>`, `<video>`, `<svg>`, `<canvas>`…) as the start of a block to drop and, with nothing closing it, dropped the rest of the message from the agent's text and from the window. A tag the message never closes is now the word the person typed (shown as ‹title›); a closed one is still dropped with its contents. Gate: test-channel-blocks ⑰.
- **A mail can no longer make the conversation jump** (security verify round 2): a mail whose style animated its own height made its row resize 60 times a second — every other message in the window jumped under the reader for as long as that mail was on screen. A formatted mail no longer animates (its keyframes, animations and transitions are removed, as mail clients do), and a row whose height keeps flipping is frozen at its last size. Gate: test-mail-frame ⑬.
- **A formatted mail is no longer cut off after you resize the window** (security verify round 2, continued): round 2's height budget took one height change per 250 ms and dropped the rest — and the mail's frame reports a height only when it changes, so the last height of any quick series (the window narrowed by a drag, two pictures arriving together after Show pictures) was never applied: measured in chrome, a 40 px narrowing reported 677 then 696 px, the row stayed at 677 and the mail's last line was hidden with no way to scroll to it. A held height now lands when the 250 ms gap ends. Gate: test-mail-frame ⑬ (the trailing edge's table, a burst on a fake clock, the wiring, a copy of the round-2 budget ending the drag at 677) + test-channels-aggregate-ui ⑩x (the window narrowed in 12 steps, the row at the last reported height).
- **A formatted mail on screen is never a blank box** (security verify round 2, continued): at most six mail frames were live at once, and the six were cut from the mails ON SCREEN too — in a thread of short HTML replies more than six fit in the window, and the rest (measured in chrome: the NEWEST three of nine, where the conversation opens) stayed empty boxes with their text hidden, for good. Every mail on screen is now shown; only the mails just above and below the window are limited. Gate: test-mail-frame ⑦ (the tables + a copy of the old verdict blanking a visible row) + test-channels-aggregate-ui ⑩ⓗ / ⑩x (every formatted row on screen live at every stop, up to 10 on screen in the attack room).
- **A very large mail body is no longer downloaded whole before it is refused** (security verify round 2): the attachment route sends no `Content-Length` (a piped file stream is chunked), so round 1's "refuse before the download" never engaged and every client pulled the whole body (up to 100 MB) into memory on every open of the conversation before judging its size. The formatted view now reads the body up to its 2 MB bound and stops there (the stream is cancelled), and the route says the file's size. Gate: test-mail-frame ⑫ (a 3 MB chunked body refused after ≤ bound + one chunk, the stream cancelled; a lying header never trusted; a copy without the running bound reads it whole).
- **Lark messages no longer show raw tags** (飞书消息里不再出现 `<p>` 这种原始标签). The owner: "lark 有些消息里混入了 <p> 这种 raw tag". A message an integration posted as HTML becomes paragraphs and line breaks, **bold** and *italic* are shown as such, links are real links, mentions are chips; anything else that looks like a tag is stripped to its words — a lone `<placeholder>` a person typed is shown as ‹placeholder›. This also applies to messages already stored (read the new way when shown) and to what an agent reads. Code blocks and inline code stay exactly as written.
- **Lark cards show what is in them** — the card's title, its text, dividers, notes and button labels — instead of only "[card] title".
- **A Lark bot has a name** (飞书机器人显示名字而不是 "app"). The owner: "lark 里还有标记为 app 的情况，其实是个 bot 应该是有名字的". VibeSpace asks Lark for the application's name (the app needs the permission `admin:app.info:readonly`; without it the row says "Bot" and the last four characters of the bot's id — never "app"), and the name has a small bot mark beside it. Messages stored earlier are named the same way when shown.
- Under the hood: PURE `src/mail-frame.js` (the allowlist re-serializer, the DOMPurify config, the CSP, the Show-pictures rule, the parent's message verdict, the lazy-frame rule) + `src/lib/channel-mail-frame.js` (the channel surface's ONE srcdoc); Gmail keeps the text/html part as the record's `role: 'body'` attachment, written into the attachment cache at ingest from the thread read it already made (zero extra vendor units) and read through the existing attachment route; `Content-ID` rides as `attachments[].cid`. The Lark markup reader lives in `src/channel-blocks.js` (`markupRead`, `larkMdBlocks`, `larkCardBlocks`, the `sealTags` wall); the record schema gains the `i` (italic) run, the `hr` block and a card's inner `blocks`. The bot name: a tenant token + `GET /open-apis/application/v6/applications/:app_id`, paced and metered, cached per app id for 6 h with its refusal (said once in the log); the engine's one read hook `recordView` names bots and reads markup in records stored earlier (the store is never rewritten).
- Gates: **test-mail-frame** (new, fast: a 58-mail hostile corpus — scripts in every spelling, meta refresh, base, forms, embedded frames, srcdoc and `</iframe>` / `</style>` breakouts, `javascript:` in every attribute and entity spelling, SVG / MathML, CSS `url()` / `@import` / `image-set` — nothing survives and the output is a fixed point; a 10 MB body refused by name; 1 000 pictures capped; the CSP exact; the Show-pictures and message-verdict tables; three weakened-sanitizer controls RED); test-channel-record ⑦ (the Lark tag census: the store's `<p>` / `<country>` shapes, every element tag the adapter reads and hostile markup — no `<…>` in `rec.text` or any block, new and stored; a control) and ⑧ (the ONE sandboxed frame, pinned by name, with three controls); test-channels-lark-shape ⑤b (the bot name: resolved, refused → "Bot ····", from a mention, cached, metered, the stored view; a pre-lane control); test-channels-gmail-shape (the body kept at ingest, served with zero vendor calls; `cid`; single-part HTML); test-channels-aggregate-ui ⑩ (heavy: the formatted frame in chrome — sandboxed and opaque, remote pictures not requested until Show pictures, the toggle, a hostile mail reaching nothing — a local beacon never hit, with a raw-render control that does hit it — a spoofed resizer message ignored, ≤ 6 live frames over 32 mails, the phone width, the bot mark); test-channel-window-render's hostile Lark legs now expect markup READ, not printed.

### A quote is a quote, a topic is a topic (the owner, 2026-09-28: "都是")

- **A Lark reply made without "reply in thread" is a quote, not a thread.** It stays in the conversation with a small strip of the message it quotes above it (the author and the start of the text; click it to jump there) — no "in thread" tag, no thread pane, and the message it quotes no longer grows a "3 条回复" chip. Only a real topic (a topic group's message, or a reply made in the thread) has the chip, the "在话题中" tag and the pane. So a reply you approved as "引用回复 (shown in the chat)" is shown as exactly that once it is sent. A quote that someone later answers in a thread becomes that topic's first message and gets its chip.
- **In Chinese a thread is now "话题"** (Lark's own word), never "线程", everywhere in Channels: the chip, the tag, the pane's title, the reply box, where a reply lands, the refusals, the settings. Japanese keeps "スレッド".
- An agent reads a quote as `↳ quotes Ada: "…" (id …)` (never "in thread"); asking to read or load a quote's "thread" says it has none, without asking the channel.
- **只有真正的话题里的新消息会叫醒 agent；别人引用你的消息仍会。** The Notify… rule "is in a thread I am in" now wakes an agent only for a new message in a real topic it (or you) took part in — never for a chain of quotes; a quote of your (or the agent's) own message still wakes it, and says so: "quoted your message" / 引用了你的消息. Both rules now read "replies to or quotes a message of mine" and "is in a thread I am in, or quotes a message of mine". The daily wake cap is unchanged.

### Threads (the owner, 2026-09-28: "我发现你似乎不支持 lark 的内嵌回复 (thread) 功能")

- **A reply shows what it answers** — one line above it, `↩ Ada: 周会改到几点？`. Click it and the original message flashes (if it is further up, the window pages up to it; if it is older than everything loaded, or was never stored, it says so). A message that sits inside a thread carries a small "在话题中 / in thread" tag.
- **A thread opens beside the list** on a desktop and as a full page with a Back button on a phone — never unfolded inside the list, never saved in the layout. The root message's chip says "3 条回复 · 最近 5m". Lark does not return a topic's replies with the group's messages, so a topic nobody opened here says "在话题中 · 打开以加载"; opening it loads its replies (at most once a minute per thread; only while you have it open — never on a timer).
- **Reply in a thread**: the pane has its own box ("在话题中回复…" — "落在此话题内"), keeps a separate draft per thread, and can answer one reply inside the thread. A Lark group that does not allow topic replies says so, and your text is kept.

### Reactions ("以及 reaction (附加在消息上的表情)")

- Emoji chips under each message: the emoji, the count, yours highlighted; hover (or long-press on a phone) shows who. Click a chip to add or remove yours — it changes when the channel answers, never on a guess, and a click is never sent twice. `+` opens a picker (a quick row, search, the channel's own emoji; arrows + Enter). Custom emoji are drawn through VibeSpace, never loaded from the vendor's address. Another person's (or another tab's) reaction appears on the chip in place — the list is not redrawn.
- **Cost:** reactions are read only for the messages on your screen, at most 20 list calls a minute per account, and before the new-message budget — scrolling fast through a busy group cannot slow new messages. Three new settings under Channels (reactions per minute, minutes a list stays fresh, seconds between two loads of one thread).
- **Lark:** adding and removing reactions works with your current sign-in. SEEING who reacted needs one more Lark permission (`im:message.reactions:read`), and the sign-in now asks for it by default ("Also read who reacted" is on) — if your Lark app already has it enabled, ONE Re-authorize is all it takes; until then the account card, the window's line and the reaction `+` say "Reactions can be read after one Re-authorize". If Lark refuses the sign-in because the app has not enabled that permission (Lark's page shows error 20027), the sign-in dialog offers one "Sign in without im:message.reactions:read" and the account then says "Lark refused im:message.reactions:read — enable it in the app console and Re-authorize" — it never narrows the sign-in without saying so. Pressing Deny on Lark's page now ends the sign-in and says so (it used to report "connected" in the tab and wait ten minutes).

### Agents

- `vibespace-channels read` now shows each message's place and its reactions as words — `↳ replying to A: "…" (id om_x1) · in thread omt_t1`, `[thread omt_t1 · 3 replies · last 5 min ago]`, `reactions: 👍 3 (the account owner)` — never who reacted. `read --thread <id>` shows one thread from what is stored (it never loads one); `refresh --thread <id>` loads it.
- `reply --to <id>` answers a message and `--in-thread` puts the answer inside its thread (the approval card says "Reply in thread — under Ada: …"); see "Where a reply lands" below.
- `react` / `unreact` PROPOSE a reaction, like a reply. Each account's new "Agent reactions" setting (Edit dialog): "You approve each one" (the default), "As the channel policy allows", or "Off". The card reads "Worker wants to react 👍 to Ada: "…"" with Approve / Reject; the agent hears the result in one line with its next message. A reaction never wakes anyone — reactions on an agent's message reach it as one line in its next turn (at most one per message per hour).
- **Wake an agent when someone replies to it** only if you ask: Notify… has two new rules, "replies to or quotes a message of mine" and "is in a thread I am in, or quotes a message of mine". By default a reply to an agent waits for its next turn at no cost.

### Where a reply lands (the owner, 2026-09-28: "the boolean is Lark-shaped")

- **Every reply says where it will land**, on the approval card, in the Outbox and on the agent's tool card: "引用回复 — 回复 Ada：…" (a quote, shown in the chat), "在话题中回复 — 位于 Ada 之下：…" (inside the thread), or "在话题中回复，并同时显示在聊天中" (inside the thread and also in the chat — Slack's way; Lark does not offer it). A plain message says nothing extra. The tool-card row says "起草了一条引用回复 / 在话题中起草了一条回复".
- **An agent names only the message and the channel's own habit decides**: `vibespace-channels reply <conv> "…" --to <id>` answers a message that is already inside a thread in that thread (it cannot be quoted from the main list), and a message outside a thread the way the channel usually does — Lark and Telegram quote it, Slack would thread it; Gmail quotes. `--in-thread` puts it in the thread, `--also-in-chat` in the thread and the chat. The agent is told which one it got and why ("lands in a thread — the default: that message is already in a thread").
- **A placement the channel does not offer is refused before anything is drafted**, in words that list what the channel does offer ("a reply in a thread that is also shown in the chat is not offered on this channel — offered here: chat, quote, thread"); nothing waits for your approval. Quoting a message that sits inside a thread is refused the same way.
- Drafts made before this change keep working: a draft that said "in a thread" is read as a thread reply and sent that way. `--reply-to` still works as the old name of `--to`, and `--in-thread <id>` still names the message.

### Fixed after a fresh-eyes walk (2026-09-28)

- A thread (or Refresh) on a **disabled** account said "Lark / 飞书 is disabled" in English on a Chinese or Japanese page; it now says, in your language, that the account is disabled and where to enable it.
- In a thread you cannot answer (a read-only or disabled account, a group without topic replies) each reply showed a "reply to this message" arrow that did nothing — on a phone it was always visible. It is no longer drawn there.
- **Who reacted** now lists names only: your own reaction says "You" (it used to show your account's internal id, like `ou_3f1a…` on Lark), and people the conversation has no name for are counted in "and N more" instead of appearing as ids (or as "unknown" on a long press).
- A reaction on an agent's message now waits above its composer as **"a reaction notice"** (it said "a channel message"), and the agent is no longer told to answer it with `vibespace-channels reply`.
- When an agent asks for a reply placement the channel does not offer, the refusal now also says which flags ask for what IS offered ("ask for what is offered with: chat: leave out --to · quote: --to <msg id>") — it used to name only "chat, quote", which is not something the agent can type.
- On a phone, the thread's reply box no longer cuts its line "lands inside this thread · sent at once, as you" (in Japanese the "sent at once" half was cut off); it wraps.

### Under the hood

- **Reply placements (2026-09-28):** each channel declares where a reply may land in its `threads` capability row — `placements` (chat / quote / thread / thread+chat) and `rootReply` (its norm for a message outside a thread) — checked when the channel registers (an incoherent row does not load) and counted by a census over every channel; the outbox policy decides a draft's placement from that row and one local fact (is the answered message inside a thread) with no call to the vendor; a channel is only ever handed a placement it declared (anything else is refused before the request). The fake channel offers all four.
- ONE model for Lark, Slack and Telegram: a record's place (`replyTo`, `threadKey`, new optional `root`) with threads DERIVED from the stored messages (never stored), reactions as an append-only side log folded when read; two new capability rows (`threads`, `reactions`) gate every control — never an adapter's name. The side log lives beside each conversation's messages (`msgs/<account>/~side/`), is trimmed with them, and never feeds search or the wake funnel (test-architecture §64 walks the code from every side-record write and proves no path reaches a wake).
- Every peer-written field is bounded before it is parsed (an emoji name, a glyph, a reaction list, a thread id; a reply chain stops after 64 hops and a cycle ends at once).
- **Verify r1 (money / the event loop):** a reaction event on a message VibeSpace never stored used to search every message log of the account, once per event, and never remembered the miss (Lark sends one for every message of every chat the bot is in); a miss is now remembered for 10 minutes and the search runs at most 30 times a minute per account — the rest are dropped by name, every one still acknowledged.
- **Verify r1 (money / the event loop):** a reaction storm on one message used to grow its side log without bound (it was compacted only when a MESSAGE trim ran) and every page read and every live update then read the whole file, twice, on the event loop; the log now compacts itself past 1 MiB, a read takes the newest 2 MiB only, one read per page, and an event naming a conversation for a message it never held writes nothing.
- **Verify r1 (the parser census):** every new function that reads peer-written data now has a size bound checked with an oversize input and, where its work grows with the input, a linear-time pin (twice the input may cost at most 2.5 times as long). It found the side log's compaction quadratic in the number of distinct emoji on one message (16 000 took 143 ms) and writing a compacted line far past its 8 KiB bound; it is linear now and keeps the first 64 emoji, marked truncated.
- **Verify r1 (money / the event loop):** a busy room whose reactions had all been read (one list per message, 5 000 messages) kept its side log past the compaction trigger, so every new reaction event re-read and re-wrote the whole file (43 ms each) and a new reaction on an old message was never shown; the compacted log now keeps the most recently changed messages within 512 KiB (older ones are read again when a window shows them), so a compaction is hundreds of kilobytes of events apart.
- **Verify r1 (identity):** an agent whose access to a conversation you removed no longer hears about new reactions on the messages it sent there (it kept receiving the counts, the conversation's name and the message id).
- **Verify r1 (identity):** a thread is loaded only under a key the conversation itself names — `refresh X --thread <a thread id of chat Y>` used to fetch chat Y's replies into X (Lark answers a thread listing by its id whatever chat is named) where an agent allowed to read X alone could read them; now it is refused by name with no vendor call, and Lark drops any listed message whose `chat_id` is another chat's.
- **Verify r2 (money):** a thread with more than 500 replies used to be walked back to its 500th reply every time its pane opened or refreshed (four or more Lark calls instead of one, every minute the pane stayed open), and its pane never showed the replies past the 500th; the walk now stops at the newest reply it already has and the pane opens on the newest replies, paging back to the first.
- **Verify r2 (identity):** removing an agent's access while one of its requests was waiting on Lark (loading a thread, refreshing, preparing a reaction or a reply in a thread, searching) no longer lets that request finish for it — it gets the same "not found" as any conversation it cannot see, and no draft is created in its name.
- **Verify r2 (identity):** when you remove an agent's access to a conversation and then approve or reject a proposal it made there, the agent is told only the outcome ("proposal … SENT — you no longer have access to that conversation") — no longer the conversation's name, the id of the message that was sent or the thread it landed in; `vibespace-channels status` shows those proposals the same way. Your Outbox still shows them whole.
- **Verify r2 (money, the cost census):** every read of a conversation's reaction log now reads at most its newest 2 MiB (the last whole-file reads are gone), and a compaction the disk refuses is retried after another 512 KiB of reactions instead of on every reaction; a new gate measures 100 reaction events on 1, 2 and 4 MiB logs (bytes read per event stay flat, twice the log never costs more than 2.5 times the time).
- **Verify r2 (money):** a custom emoji picture the channel refuses (deleted, too large) is asked for once and remembered — it used to be fetched again every time its chip was drawn — and a "too many requests" answer to one picture makes the account's other pictures wait, like attachments already did.
- **Verify r2 (money):** when Lark answers "too many requests" to a reaction list, the reactions of the next rows you scroll to wait for the time Lark asked for instead of being asked again at once (each of those calls also used up part of the minute's budget for new messages); while the account is waiting, the rows are not marked as recently asked, so they load as soon as the wait is over.
- **Verify r3 (identity):** what waits for an agent's next message — a channel message it was notified about, the receipt of a proposal it made, a reaction count on its message — is checked again when that message is sent: if you removed the agent's access to the conversation in between, the agent gets only its own proposal's outcome ("proposal … SENT — you no longer have access to that conversation") and nothing the conversation said. It used to receive all of it whole while `vibespace-channels read` already answered "not found".
- **Verify r3:** a thread load that was cut short (a network error, the minute's budget) and then a VibeSpace restart no longer leaves a gap in the thread for good: where the load stopped is saved, and the next load reads back to it (it used to read only what was newer than the last reply it had, and the replies in between were never loaded).
- **Verify r3:** scrolling up in a Lark thread now loads its older replies (it used to ask Lark for the newest page again and show nothing more — replies older than the newest 50 could not be seen). Each scroll-up brings the next 50, up to the newest 200 Lark lists for a thread; past that the pane says the older replies cannot be loaded here, and once the start is reached it stops asking. Scrolling up right after opening a thread ("paused for a moment") no longer stops the pane from loading older replies later.
- **Verify r3 (money):** when a conversation's cached "what can I do here" answer has gone stale, the reactions of 20 rows appearing at once ask Lark for it once, not 20 times.
- **Verify r3 (memory):** what VibeSpace remembers per account about reactions and threads (when each message's reactions were last read, the ids of your own reactions, when each thread was last loaded) no longer grows for as long as the server runs: at most 20 000 / 20 000 / 5 000 rows per account, anything untouched for 30 days forgotten (forgetting costs one extra read later, never a wrong answer).
- **Verify r3 (money):** in a Lark group whose messages carry many reactions (an announcement everyone acknowledges), loading the reactions of the rows on screen could use Lark's whole minute of requests — each list of more than 50 reactions is several requests — and new messages then waited a minute; the reaction limit now counts requests, so new messages always keep two thirds of the minute. Rows past the limit are loaded a minute later.
- ~~**Verify r2:** the "is in a thread I am in" rule now also fires for a reply to a reply of the agent's own message when that message itself is not stored in the conversation~~ — superseded by the owner's decision above: a chain of quotes is not a thread (a quote of the agent's message still wakes it).
- Gates: test-channel-placement (new, fast — the placement table per channel incl. Slack / Telegram rows, the capability census, the send contract, the engine end to end, the words in zh / ja / en, five patched-copy controls), test-channel-thread, test-channel-reactions (new, fast), test-channel-outbox §6 (the reaction proposal through every state), test-channels-engine ⑰ ⑱ ⑲ (⑲ = one revoke, every channel), test-channel-drain rule 20, test-architecture §64 / §64b / §65 (§65 = the access gate census: every agent answer, stash producer, owner surface and CLI path); test-channel-threads-ui (new, heavy — real chrome over the fake adapter).

### Lark: one search finds every new message — groups, single chats and thread replies (the owner, 2026-09-28)

(lane lark-search-poll, B-5aab — the owner, 2026-09-28: "从 lark pull 消息可以通过搜索空格+时间范围来搜索最近所有新消息吧，这样也顺便能解决私聊问题". Built on the threads-and-reactions lane.)

- **One search instead of one read per chat.** Every 30 seconds a Lark account asks Lark's message search (an empty query over a time window) which conversations have new messages, then reads only those. One request covers the whole account — groups, single chats and thread replies. The search's snippet is never used as the message: the words always come from the chat's own history.
- **Your single chats show up.** The first search after you connect (or re-authorize) also lists the single chats of the last 7 days, as already read — nobody is woken for them ("Found 4 single chats from the last 7 days"). A new message in a single chat afterwards is unread, named by the person ("Ann", else "Single chat" — never a raw id; the name is shown as plain text, with hidden direction-reversing and invisible characters removed, and never reaches an agent as an instruction), and on the first screen it wears "DM · 1 new" (单聊 · 1 条新消息).
- **Agents:** handing a whole Lark account to an agent includes your single chats — it can read them and is woken on them (your decision). Handing one chat works as before.
- **Checked less often only when proven.** Until the search has found at least 200 messages with at most 2 % missed — measured for at least one full 15-minute cycle, so a chat the search never sees has been read on its own and counted — every chat is still polled at its usual pace. Then each chat is checked at least every 5 minutes (setting "Once the search finds everything…", 300 s), an open window keeps 30 s, and the chat's freshness says "within 90 s". If the search starts missing messages, the usual pace comes back by itself and the card says so with the numbers.
- **The account card** says what the search is doing ("New messages: a search every 30 s · each chat is still checked on its own until 200 messages show it finds everything (57/200)", "…each chat is also checked every 5 min", "Lark is limiting the search · resuming in 12 s", "Search is off: Lark refused search:message — enable it in the app console, publish a version, then Re-authorize") and ONE line with ONE Re-authorize for everything the sign-in lacks: "One Re-authorize adds: reading reactions · new-message search and single chats".
- **Signing in:** the default sign-in now also asks for `search:message` and `im:message.p2p_msg:get_as_user` (account option "New-message search", on by default). If Lark refuses because your app has not enabled one of them (error 20027), each retry drops ONE permission, least important first — reading reactions, then reading single chats, then the search — each on a button that names it.
- **Cost:** a quiet account spends 2 requests a minute on the search, at most 10 a minute in a burst (a tenth of Lark's shared 100/min), inside the account's own budget and pace; a search refused, limited or DOWN on Lark's side never pauses the account's normal reading (the card says "Lark search is not answering — each chat is checked on its own"); an account whose sign-in lacks `search:message` sends no search at all. New settings under Channels: seconds between searches (30), seconds each search re-reads (60), days of single chats found at first (7), seconds between checks once proven (300).
- **Names are cleaned everywhere.** A person's display name, a mention, an attachment's file name, a chat's title, a reactor — every name Lark, Gmail or a stranger chose — now has its direction-override and invisible characters and any control characters removed before it is shown or handed to an agent (a name could reverse the words after it, hide a tag from the frame check, or read as nobody).
- **A hidden character no longer hides a tag.** A message whose text spells one of VibeSpace's own instruction tags with a zero-width, direction-control or control character inside it is now neutered like the plain tag before any agent reads it — a message stored before this update included; the rest of the message keeps its characters.
- **A tag split across lines no longer comes alive in an agent's wake.** The message an agent is woken with quotes each line of a chat message; a stranger who ended one line with the start of an instruction tag had the next line's quote mark close it. Each line is now checked on its own.
- **Under the hood:** a new PURE module `src/channel-feed.js` (the window, the page's trust check — a search that ignores its time window is stopped after one page — the fold into durable "owed" marks, the coverage measurement), drain rule 21 (one search page = one scheduled vendor call), channel-caps `feedState` (the one answer "is the search carrying this account"), the registry's `changeFeed` capability row; the engine writes every owed mark to disk BEFORE it moves the search's cursor, so a crash costs a re-read, never a message. Gates: test-channel-feed (new), test-channel-drain (rule 21 in the seeded walk + a table + 5 mutants), test-channel-caps, test-channel-adapter-contract, test-channels-lark-shape, test-oauth-loopback, test-channels-engine, test-channels-focus, test-channel-filter; heavy test-channels-aggregate ⑫ (the owner's 873 conversations).

### Pairing that says where and why (lane-pairing, B-7007 — the owner's MacBook, 2026-09-27)

- **Pick the address the device dials.** "Pair a device" lists every address this VibeSpace can name for itself — the one your browser is using now (first), the relay, this machine's Tailscale / LAN / public addresses, its hostname, IPv6 — each saying who can reach it, plus **Custom…** (checked as you type: a path, a query or a strange scheme is refused right there). The command's two URLs both use the address you picked. (Before: one address — the relay — which the Mac's network could not reach.) The ssh machine's "Upgrade to dial-out" uses the same list.
- **Opening the dialog never replaces the command.** A new token is made only when you press **Create pairing** or **Generate a new command**, and the latter says "the one you generated before stops working now". The machine row's pairing icon opens a sheet that first shows whether the device ever connected. (Before: every re-open silently made a new token, so the device kept dialing with an old one.)
- **A device that is not connected says why.** Its row, the Machines card and the pairing sheet read one state: "Connected since 09:41 — before that 3 attempts failed (token mismatch)", "Last dial: refused (token mismatch) at 23:12 — the device holds an older command; generate a new one", "Connected, but the device refuses this server's key", "Offline since … — no dial attempt has reached this server since", "Never connected — the command generated at … has not reached this server". The Machines card's **Dial history…** shows the device's own last 20 attempts. (Before: "offline", while the server log said "token mismatch".)
- **The install command checks the address before it installs anything** and stops with the reason: this device cannot resolve the host, `wss://` to a plain port, nothing answers, not a VibeSpace address, or the command is older than the pairing — "✗ nothing was installed". (Before: a typo address was installed and dialed forever.) `--no-check` skips it.
- **Long device folders work on macOS**: the device's socket moves to a short per-user path when the natural one would exceed macOS's 104-byte limit (the relay-named folder made it 106 — the device never started listening).
- The device writes every dial outcome to `state/dial-status.json` and one log line naming the reason ("dial-out failed — dns: …", "dial-out refused — token-mismatch: …"); a refused dial now receives the server's reason; an address that never answers gives up after 15 s instead of hanging.

### Exit access: who can use a paired machine (lane-pairing ⑥)

- **The machine row's exit icon opens "Who can use Macbook?"** with two separate lists — **Borrow its network** (an agent points one command at the machine's network) and **Run commands on it** (a shell command on the machine, as you, up to 30 s) — each **Nobody**, **All my conversations** or **Only these** (conversations and Task Groups; a Task Group means every conversation in it, now or later), and **Ask me each time** for commands. The Machines card has the same **Who can use it…**. The row says what is allowed and the last command that ran ("Last run: ping -c1 … — ops, 3 min ago, exit 0").
- **Ask me each time** puts "Allow "ops" to run a command on Macbook?" in For you with the whole command and **Allow / Deny** on the row itself (the popup, the For-you window, the phone); nothing runs until you answer, and after 60 s it is refused. An agent cannot answer it.
- **Every command an agent runs on a machine is recorded**: a card in its chat ("Machines · Macbook — ran `ping -c1 10.0.0.5` on Macbook — exit 0 · 1.2 s", or why it did not run), a line in `data/exit-audit.jsonl`, and the row's last run. A command already running when you remove access finishes and says so.
- **Agents see only what they may use**: `vibespace-exit list` shows only the machines open to that conversation ("network: yes · commands: ask"); a refusal says which permission is missing and that you can change it under "Who can use it" — never another conversation's name. Background Work jobs can never use an exit.
- **Nothing changes by itself**: a machine that had "Allow as exit" on is open to all conversations for both; one that had it off is open to nobody (migration `2026-09-exit-access-lists`; the old values are archived under `data/archive/`).
- **The run limit is 30 s — and always was.** The exit route promised 120 s, but the device daemon has always stopped a command at 30 s and reported it as "exit 1"; the limit is now one number everywhere (the daemon, the CLI's help, the card), and a command stopped by it says "timed out after 30 s".

### Under the hood

- **Verify round 1 (B8): "Generate a new command" locks out whoever holds the previous one — unless you choose otherwise.** The connected device used to receive the new command over its link automatically, so the sentence "the one you generated before stops working now" did not hold for a device that was dialed in — and a rotation is also how a leaked command is retired (reproduced: a daemon started from the old command received the rotated token and was accepted again). While a device is connected, the pairing sheet now offers "Send the new command to the connected device over its link" — unchecked by default; unchecked, the holder is locked out (since verify round 2: disconnected at once — see B8-r2 below) and the row says so ("refused (token mismatch)"), checked, the trusted device follows without running anything. Gates: test-dial-facts (the PURE verdict, wiring pins, a push-always control copy) + test-pair-dialog-ui (a real connected daemon: locked out by default, updated in place when asked).
- **Verify round 1 (A3): borrowing a machine's network needs the conversation's own credentials.** The forward is a loopback port on the hub, and the "Borrow its network" list gated only who may OPEN it — any local process, an unlisted conversation's shell included, could point `curl --proxy socks5h://127.0.0.1:<port>` at it once a listed one had (reproduced). `vibespace-exit use / url` now hand out `socks5h://<user>:<pass>@127.0.0.1:<port>` — a SOCKS5 username/password pair minted per conversation and machine (the same pair on every `use` while the grant holds), demanded by the port before a byte reaches the machine; removing a conversation from the list drops its pair and cuts its connections while the other holders keep theirs. Tools that will not send SOCKS5 credentials are refused with "no acceptable authentication method" (curl, git and every libcurl tool do; `vibespace-exit run` remains the universal way). Gates: test-exit-proxy (a SOCKS-auth client: bare / no-auth / wrong password / unknown user refused, two conversations' pairs, a revoke, a no-gate control copy) — and reproduced end to end with real curl over a real daemon's SOCKS.
- **Verify round 1 (A1, A5): the exit audit holds the whole command; a cut output says so; the exit code is always a number.** The audit line cut a command at 120 characters — a 4 KB command's payload past that head was in no record at all (the row and the card keep their short heads by design). A command whose output the machine cut (1 MiB of stdout, 64 KiB of stderr, or its 2 MiB buffer) came back as a clean exit 0 with the tail silently missing; now the reply, the audit line and the CLI's closing line say "OUTPUT CUT". And an output over the 2 MiB buffer answered the string `ERR_CHILD_PROCESS_STDIO_MAXBUFFER` as the exit code, on which `vibespace-exit`'s own exit threw a stack trace — the daemon answers a number, the manager and the CLI coerce whatever an older daemon sends. Gates: test-exit-reach (the whole command on record + a 120-char control copy, the string-code and the cut shapes through the real manager, wiring pins) + test-agentd-dial (a real daemon: 1.5 MB cut and named, 3 MB numeric code).
- **Verify round 1 (C2): a device that holds another command's host key stays dialed in and its row says so.** The server used to close the link the moment the device refused its key, the device re-dialed a second later and was accepted again — `hosts.json` rewritten and every client repainted once a second, forever, while the row read "Offline — no dial attempt has reached this server" (measured: 75 dial-ins in 75 s, the row wrong 149 of 150 samples). The link is now kept unauthenticated: the row reads "the device refuses this server's key" steadily, every operation on it is refused at once with the way out ("generate a new command and run it there"), and a fresh dial-in or a minute later is asked again. Gates: new fast test-dial-link-kept (the real DeviceManager + deviceForDial over a fake refusing daemon, a no-keep control copy) + test-agentd-dial's attack-18 leg (a real daemon: still on the same link 4 s later, the row steady).
- **Verify round 1 (B9): a second machine running a copy of a device's pairing no longer fights the first one every second.** Run the same install command on two machines — or migrate a Mac's home folder to a new one — and both daemons dialed in as the same device: each connection knocked the other off, once a second, forever; the row flipped between "connected" and "1 attempt failed", every client repainted twice a second, and nothing said what was going on. Now the first device keeps its link: the second is refused by name ("pair this machine under its own name — another device is dialed in as … and answering"), its daemon backs off to a retry every 30 s, and the machine row says "Another device is also dialing in as this one (from …)" for ten minutes. When the first device goes away, the second gets in on its next attempt. Gates: test-dial-facts (the verdict table + a control), test-agentd-dial (two real daemons on one pairing, with a no-boot-id copy as the control).
- **Verify round 2 (B9-r2a): a second dial-in is judged by whether the first still answers — never by a header it can leave out.** Round 1 admitted a newcomer that carried no boot id unasked ("a daemon from before this release: replaced as before"), so a copy of a device's pairing on an old bundle — or any client that simply strips the header — knocked the live device off at will (reproduced with two real daemons: 9 accepts, 8 closes in 8 s). A boot id is a claim the server cannot check; whether the current link answers, it can. Now only the same known boot id (the daemon re-dialing after its own drop) is admitted unasked; every other newcomer, with or without an id, is refused while the current device answers and admitted when it stays silent. The check also joins a hello still in flight instead of reading it as "not connected ⇒ dead" — a newcomer arriving inside that round trip used to evict a healthy device. Gates: test-dial-facts (the cells + a control copy with round 1's rule), test-dial-link-kept (the real gate over an answering daemon: a header-less newcomer refused, the hello-in-flight window, a silent current replaced, a closed-world control under round 1's rule), test-agentd-dial (two real daemons: the header-less copy refused, and the flap back under a patched server as the control).
- **Verify round 2 (B8-r2): "Generate a new command" disconnects the device holding the old one at once.** Round 1 refused that device only "at its next dial" and left its link up — so a retired command's holder (an impostor, a lost laptop) stayed fully able to act until it happened to drop, and worse, the duplicate-device rule then refused YOUR device running the new command as the intruder while the old holder answered (reproduced with two real daemons: four refusals in nine seconds, the row saying "another device is also dialing in as this one"). Now the mint ends the holder's link (its next dial is refused by name), the sheet says "the device that was connected has been disconnected; it holds the previous command, which no longer works", and the device on the new command gets straight in. Choosing "send the new command to the connected device" keeps the link — and only while the hand-over lands. Gates: test-dial-facts (wiring + words), test-agentd-dial (a real holder cut at the mint and refused on its re-dial, the new device admitted; a no-lockout control copy brings round 1's shape back), test-pair-dialog-ui (the sentence).
- **Verify round 2 (A3-r2): a borrowed network is checked on every connection, not only when the pair is handed out.** Round 1's per-conversation SOCKS5 credentials were checked as a pair only, and a pair lived until the forward stopped — so a conversation removed from a Task Group that granted it (the machine's list untouched), or one that had ended, could keep opening connections through the machine with the pair it already had (reproduced). Now every connection also asks whether that conversation is still running and still allowed on that machine right now; a conversation's end (killed or exited) drops its pair and cuts its open connections at once, and a forward nobody holds any more is closed. The password compare is constant-time. Gates: test-exit-proxy (a Task Group left, a dead conversation, the cut, the stop, the wiring of both session-end paths, a pair-only control copy).
- **Verify round 2 (ask-a): an "ask me each time" request whose conversation has ended runs nothing.** Round 1 judged "is this conversation still allowed?" after your Allow — but it asked the conversation object it had in hand, so a conversation killed or ended while its request waited still had its command run on the machine when you pressed Allow (reproduced). Now a conversation's end settles its waiting requests at once (the item says "the conversation ended before you answered"), an Allow for a conversation that is gone is refused by name and runs nothing, and a `vibespace-exit run` that gives up (its process ended, its own timeout) withdraws its request the same way. Gates: test-exit-reach (the stale Allow, the kill path, the call's end, the route with a client that hangs up; a no-liveness control copy).
- **Verify round 2 (ask-b): ticking an "Allow … to run a command?" item off IS the answer.** Round 1 left the request waiting its full 60 s after you marked its For-you item done or dismissed it (or "Mark all seen", or the agent resolved its own item) — and the request could still be allowed afterwards through its id: one question, two states. Now the item leaving the list by any door settles the request at once as not allowed (the CLI hears it immediately, a later Allow is refused as already answered), and the store's own expiry sweep settles it as expired. Gates: test-exit-reach (the ✓, dismiss, Mark all seen, the agent's own resolve, the store's expiry, an Allow still working once; a no-subscription control copy), test-user-todos-expiry.
- **Verify round 2 (the open connection): removing a conversation from the Task Group that lent it a machine's network cuts its open connections at once.** Removing access in "Who can use it" always cut a conversation's open connections through the machine, and round 2 made every NEW connection check the access — but a conversation that lost the network through its Task Group (unbound from the group, the group deleted or archived, the group's folders edited) kept every connection it already had open, for as long as the agent held it (reproduced: bytes still went through the machine 1.5 s after it left the group). Now any change to the Task Groups re-checks every machine being borrowed and every waiting "ask me each time" request: a conversation that is no longer allowed loses its credentials and its open connections, a machine nobody may borrow any more stops being lent, and a waiting request is answered "not allowed" (its For-you item resolved as access removed). Gates: test-exit-proxy (an open connection cut when its conversation leaves the group, another holder untouched, the forward stopped with its last holder, the wiring; a control copy that re-judges nobody keeps the connection), test-exit-reach (a waiting request settled; a control copy without it).
- **Verify round 3 (the dial-token door census): every place a pairing secret is created, checked, logged or written goes through one door.** The pairing's two secrets are now created and checked in one place (`src/pairing-token.js`): every check compares fixed-size fingerprints in constant time (three checks — the server's dial gate, the device's check of the server, and the session bridge — compared with an ordinary string comparison, which finishes sooner the earlier two values differ; the session bridge compared the secret itself on a port any local program can reach). A secret written onto a device goes through the device's own secret channel, which creates the file readable only by its owner in one step (the in-place update wrote it and then changed its permissions). A check in the release gate fails if code anywhere creates, hashes, compares, logs or writes a pairing secret any other way, or puts one on a command line. Gates: test-dial-facts (the census, with a planted example per rule), test-dial-token-sinks.
- **Verify round 3 (B-inst): the pairing command no longer shows its secrets to other users of the device.** The command you run on a device carried both secrets as options of `bash`, so any other user of that machine could read them in its process list for the whole install (a minute or more while it sets things up), and the installer passed the dial secret the same way to two of its own steps; on Windows the device agent kept it on its command line for good. Whoever reads the dial secret can connect as that device. The command now hands the secrets to the installer in its environment (`VIBESPACE_DIAL_TOKEN=… VIBESPACE_HOST_TOKEN=… bash -s -- …`), which only the same user can read; the installer passes the dial secret only to the step that needs it and nothing it starts keeps either; on Windows the agent starts without it. Commands generated before this release still work. (A device agent started with the secret in its environment keeps its pairing when it updates itself — caught before release: the restarted agent would have overwritten the saved secret with an empty one.) Gates: test-device-install-check (every process's command line watched during a real install: no secret; the old command shape still installs; a control copy with the old steps shows the secret), test-pair-dialog-ui, test-dial-facts.
- **Verify round 3 (B-rst): a stranger at the dial endpoint can no longer stop the VibeSpace server.** The dial endpoint answers anyone who reaches the port (a device has no sign-in cookie), and this lane made it hold a refused connection open for two seconds so the device reads why — but a client that reset its connection during those two seconds (or while the server checked whether a device was already connected) raised an error nothing handled, and the server exits on such an error: one connection from anyone on the network restarted the whole server, dropping every browser (reproduced: 3 of 3). The endpoint now handles a reset connection by closing it. Gate: test-dial-link-kept (four resets at each moment the endpoint holds a connection, nothing escapes; a control copy without the fix lets all four through).
- **Verify round 3 (B-grad): "Upgrade to dial-out" no longer shows the pairing's secrets to other users of either machine.** Upgrading an ssh machine to dial-out installed the device agent over ssh with both secrets of the new pairing on the ssh command line — readable by every user of the VibeSpace machine (in its process list, for the whole install, up to 5 minutes) and of the target machine (reproduced with a stand-in `ssh`: the process list showed the dial token). Whoever reads the dial token can dial in as that machine. The secrets now travel inside the connection with the installer, never on a command line. Gates: test-dial-facts (the invocation, a control copy with the old command line), test-dial-token-sinks (new, heavy: the tokens the pairing routes mint are looked for in every process's command line, the server's log, every live update the browser receives, every file of the server and the device — found only where they belong).
- **Verify round 3 (the authority census): every way a conversation can lose a machine now ends in one re-check.** Two rounds found, one at a time, a change that took a conversation's access away without cutting what it already had open. Now every such change — the "Who can use it" dialog, a Task Group edit (unbound, deleted, archived, its folders changed), a conversation's own facts moving (a fork taking its own id, a Codex conversation starting a new thread, its folder changing), the conversation ending (killed, exited, or resumed in another window), the machine removed or un-paired, a config import — goes through the same one re-check: the conversation's open connections through the machine are cut, its waiting "ask me each time" request is answered ("not allowed" or "the conversation ended"), and the machine's row stops listing it. A new check fails the release if a future change can take access away without it. A re-pair keeps who may use the machine (it only disconnects the device that held the old command). Gate: test-exit-rejudge (the census of every such change in the code with a planted example per rule; one live leg per change; a hub restart; a control copy whose re-check does nothing).
- **Verify round 3 (A-r3a): importing a config that takes a conversation off a machine cuts its open connections at once.** A machine's "Who can use it" lists are part of its record, and Settings → Import config replaces every record — but only the "Who can use it" dialog re-checked who is borrowing the machine, so after an import that narrowed a machine's lists (or dropped the machine) a conversation kept its open connections through it and its waiting "ask me each time" request kept waiting (reproduced). Every write to the machine records — the dialog, an import, removing a machine, an upgrade's reshaping — now re-checks every borrowed machine and every waiting request: a conversation no longer allowed loses its open connections, a machine nobody may borrow stops being lent, a waiting request is answered "not allowed". Gate: test-exit-proxy (a narrowing import, an import without the machine, a removal, the wiring; a control copy whose import does not re-check keeps the connection).
- **Verify round 2 (the dial endpoint): a stranger at the dial endpoint learns nothing about which devices are paired, and cannot flood the log.** The endpoint answers anyone who reaches the port (a device has no sign-in cookie), and it answered an unknown device name "no pairing named …" but a paired one "the token does not match" — so anyone could list the device names paired here. And every refused knock wrote one journal line: 2 000 knocks from one address took 185 ms and wrote 2 000 lines (the journal's per-service burst is spent in about a second, and then it drops the lines that matter). Now both hear the same answer ("the dial token does not match the pairing on record … generate a new command in the pairing dialog, or pair again if it is no longer listed"), sent before anything is done for a paired name; the log keeps 30 lines per address (per device when a paired device dials — two devices behind the relay's one address never mute each other) and 300 per 10 minutes in all (an IPv6 /64 counts as one address), with one line saying the rest is not logged. It is only a log budget: the right token is admitted whatever the count (a lock keyed by address would let one stale device behind the relay lock every other device out), and a paired device's row still records its last refusal. A copy of a pairing sending a new boot id on every knock no longer rewrites `hosts.json` per knock (the row's 10-minute note is written once). A device name carrying a line break (`?device=x%0A…`) is logged as one line — it could forge a journal line of its own. Gates: test-dial-facts (the sentence, the address key, the budget incl. 50 000 rotating knocks; two control copies: a raw-address budget with no ceiling, a ceiling counting knocks), test-dial-link-kept (the real gate over fake sockets: one answer byte for byte, the answer before the record, ≤ 62 lines for 2 000 knocks with the row recording, two devices behind one address, the right token admitted, the duplicate note written once, a line break in the name; four control copies), test-device-install-check (`--dial-check` against an unknown name exits 14 with the same words).
- **Verify round 1 (C3): a device's own update is no longer counted as a failed connection.** When a device installed a new daemon and restarted itself, the old process saw its link close and wrote it down as a failure, so the fresh daemon's first dial-in told the server "1 attempt failed" and the row read "connected — before that 1 attempt failed (other)" after every healthy update. The re-exec now ends the link by name ("dial-out ended — self-upgrade re-exec"), records nothing and the new daemon dials in with a clean slate. Gate: test-agentd-dial's C1 leg pins the row's `lastAccept.attempt === 0` and the device file after a real self-upgrade, with a control run over a bundle that never raises the flag (the old shape comes back).
- **Verify round 1 (C1): a device whose self-upgrade never takes is upgraded at most 3 times, then kept as-is.** The 2.330.0 loop breaker counted attempts on the server's per-link object, and every fresh dial-in builds a new one — so once the handshake ran on every dial-in (this release), a device that could not converge was re-upgraded 4 times a second (measured: 180 pushes of 1.6 MB in 45 s, the daemon re-exec'ing each time). The count now lives per device (`src/server/dial-pairing.js` upgrade ledger), keyed by the bundle version, retried only after 10 min; the upgrade names the BUNDLE's own version (a server whose package.json and bundle disagree used to re-upgrade the same device at every natural restart); and the bundle's version marker is read wherever esbuild put it (it sat past the 400 000 bytes the reader looked at, so the 2.330.0 "expected = the bundle's version" defense had silently fallen back to the package version). Gates: test-agentd-upgrade-loop (fast: a fake never-converging daemon over the real Mux, four rebuilt instances, a ledger-less control) + test-agentd-dial (a real pinned daemon: ≤ 3 upgrades in 12 s, the link kept).
- **Naive-user pass (N-radio): every radio and checkbox in the pairing and "Who can use it" dialogs sits beside its words.** A dialog-wide rule stacked each label's control above its text, so every address radio floated on its own line half-way between two addresses (centred on the phone) and "Ask me each time" sat centred above its words; the rows now read as a list of choices at 1280 and 360 px (test-pair-dialog-ui / test-exit-access-ui's label census, with a patched copy of style.css as the control).
- **Naive-user pass (N-loop): a `127.0.0.1` / `localhost` address is no longer the dialog's default.** Opened from a browser on the VibeSpace machine itself — or through an ssh tunnel — the pairing dialog listed `http://127.0.0.1:3456` first and checked, as "the address you are using now": no other machine can ever dial it. It is now the last row, worded "the address you are using now — only this machine can reach it; another device cannot", and the first address a device elsewhere can reach (Tailscale, LAN, the relay…) is checked instead.
- **Naive-user pass (N-sheet): a paired device's pairing sheet checks the address that device uses.** Re-opening the sheet to generate a new command checked the dialog's first row whatever the device dialed — so "Generate a new command" with "send the new command to the connected device" wrote the browser's `127.0.0.1` into a Tailscale-paired device's configuration (reproduced in real Chrome; on a Mac that cuts the device off until someone fixes it by hand). The sheet now checks the address the device connects through (a hand-edited one too), else the one its current command was made for, and says so under that row.
- **Naive-user pass (N-row): a machine row shows the machine's name again.** At the sidebar's default width the row's eight icons took the whole row, so every paired machine's NAME was squeezed to nothing (four devices, four nameless rows), the exit / ports / new-session / unpair icons sat past the panel's edge behind a sideways scrollbar, and "Exit: network — … · commands — …" and the last run were cut mid-sentence. The icons now wrap under the name when the row is narrow, and both exit lines wrap.
- **Naive-user pass (N-ask): "Allow" / "Deny" on an agent's request to run a command look like buttons you can press.** They sat in the row's hover bar, drawn at a third of their strength until the pointer was over the row — on a 60-second decision the Allow button looked disabled — and on the phone that bar was so wide the question shrank to one word per line ("Sessi / on 2"). They are now their own line under the command, full strength.
- **Naive-user pass (N-refused): a refused device's row tells you to run the command you already have.** Right after "Generate a new command", the old device's next dial is refused and its row said "the device holds an older command; generate a new one" — so a second Generate retired the command you were about to paste, the owner's original loop. It now says "…the device still holds a command older than the one generated at 16:52: run that one on the device (or generate a new one if you no longer have it)".
- **Naive-user pass (N-ja): in Japanese, a machine nobody may use says so.** The row's summary read "出口: ネットワーク — 誰も · コマンド — 誰も" — a bare 誰も has no negation (with an affirmative it means "everyone"), on the one line that says who can use your machine; it now reads "誰も使えない", like the dialog's own choice.
- **Naive-user pass (N-greyed): "Ask me each time" no longer sits greyed out.** With "Run commands on it" set to Nobody the switch was shown disabled and did nothing when clicked; it now appears only once a list is chosen (All my conversations / Only these), live.
- **Naive-user pass (L-time): the dial state's times follow the page's language** — a Chinese or Japanese page on an English browser said "…被拒绝（令牌不匹配），04:24 PM"; it now says "16:24".
- **Verify round 4 (the receiver-fact census): every value pairing puts into a command, a file or a device now says whose fact it is.** The round's findings were one kind of mistake — a default taken from your browser or from the server while it stood for the device (the address, its system, the proxy address handed to an agent). A check now lists every place these screens read such a fact, who it belongs to and what it feeds, and fails when a new one appears undeclared; its table names, for each of the 15 values handed out, whose default it is and the test that proves it.
- **Verify round 4 (F1): a device paired through the relay keeps the relay when you generate a new command.** The pairing sheet checked "the address this device connects through" by reading the address as it reached VibeSpace — and the relay (like most reverse proxies) rewrites that to `127.0.0.1`, so every relay-paired device's sheet checked **Custom… http://127.0.0.1**, and "Generate a new command" with "send it over its link" moved the device onto its own loopback: it dialed itself and never came back (reproduced with a real device behind a relay). The device now says which address it dials on every connection, and the sheet checks that one; the row's "…on a network that reaches …" names it too, and the sheet says "last connected through" for a device that is offline.
- **Verify round 4 (F3): a VibeSpace started for this machine only (`HOST=127.0.0.1`) no longer offers addresses nobody can reach.** The pairing dialog listed every address the machine has — its Tailscale, LAN and host-name addresses — and checked the Tailscale one "reachable from your tailnet", but a server listening only on this machine refuses all of them. It now lists only addresses this VibeSpace actually listens on, says when it listens on this machine only (use the relay, or a proxy's address under Custom…), and never checks an address another device cannot reach. With the default setting an IPv6 address is no longer offered either (the server listens on IPv4 only).
- **Verify round 4 (F6): "Pair a device" says so when the name you type is already paired.** Typing the name of a device that is already paired — say, a second Mac also named "macbook" — replaced that device's pairing without a word: the device connected under that name was cut off and its command stopped working, and you learned it only afterwards. The dialog now says, as you type, that creating will replace that pairing (and disconnect the device if it is connected), the button reads **Replace its pairing**, and it points to the row's pairing icon if you only wanted a new command for that device.
- **Verify round 4 (F7): a paired device's new command comes for that device's system.** "Generate a new command" picked macOS / Linux / Windows from the computer you are browsing on, so opening VibeSpace on a Windows PC handed a paired Mac the PowerShell command. The device now tells VibeSpace its system whenever it connects, and its command is preselected for it; a device that has never connected still starts from your browser's guess.
- **Verify round 4 (F8): the pairing sheet of a device that is not connected says what "Generate a new command" will do to it — before you press it.** For a laptop that is asleep or a Mac at home, a new command retires the one on the device: it is refused when it comes back until you run the new command there. The sheet said nothing about it until after the button; it now says so above it (and, for a device that never connected, that the command made at that time stops working).
- **Verify round 4 (F2): an agent running on another machine is told it cannot borrow a network, instead of being handed an address that does not exist there.** "Borrow its network" gives the agent a proxy address on the VibeSpace machine itself; an agent whose conversation runs on a remote machine got that same address, which on its own machine points at nothing (or at something else). It is now told so, and pointed at running the command on the machine instead.
- **Verify round 4 (F4): you see the whole command an agent asks to run before you allow it.** The request in For you showed only the first 120 characters of the command, on one line, cut after three lines with nothing saying so — the rest (a last line `… | sh`) sat folded under the Allow button; and the For-you window displayed the command as formatted text, so `*` characters vanished and a `#` line became a heading. The command is now shown exactly as it will run, line by line, in a box that scrolls when it is long.
- **Verify round 4 (F5): replying "yes" to an agent's request to run a command no longer refuses it.** The request in For you offered **Reply** next to **Allow / Deny** — and a reply closes the item, which counts as "not allowed": typing "yes, allow it" DENIED the command, while the agent got your "yes" as a new message. The request now offers only Allow / Deny (the For-you window says so where the reply box would be); a reply sent anyway is refused and the request keeps waiting for your answer.
- **Verify round 5 (C1): an address only the device vouches for is shown as the device's claim.** The pairing sheet of a connected device checks the address that device says it dials — and said so as a fact ("the address this device connects through") even when VibeSpace never offered that address. Whatever holds a device's command can say anything there (a leaked command's holder dialing in while your device is away, or a cloud metadata address), and the new command fetches its installer from that address. Now the address is still checked (a device you pointed at your own proxy by hand keeps working), but when it is neither one of this VibeSpace's addresses nor the one the current command was made for, it reads "the address this device says it connects through — VibeSpace did not offer it: check it is yours before you run the command", in the warning colour.
- **Verify round 5 (C2): a refused knock can no longer put its words on your device's row.** Anyone who knows a device's name can knock at the dial address with a wrong command; the refusal was recorded on the device together with the address and system the knock claimed, and the row's address came from the knock first. A refusal now records only that it happened (when, from where, why); what a dial says about itself is kept only from a dial that holds the pairing.
